detail:
The CDC's diagnosis guidance states that ME/CFS cannot be confirmed by any single laboratory test. Clinicians diagnose it from the history and examination using the 2015 Institute of Medicine criteria: a substantial reduction in activity lasting more than 6 months with profound fatigue, post-exertional malaise (PEM), and unrefreshing sleep, plus cognitive impairment and/or orthostatic intolerance.

PEM, a worsening of symptoms after physical, mental, or emotional exertion that often begins 12 to 48 hours later, is a hallmark that separates ME/CFS from many other fatiguing illnesses. Because many conditions can cause fatigue, evaluation also includes tests to identify other explanations before the diagnosis is settled.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about evaluation for persistent, unexplained fatigue.
summary: The CDC explains that no single test confirms ME/CFS. Diagnosis rests on the 2015 Institute of Medicine criteria: more than 6 months of profound fatigue, post-exertional malaise, and unrefreshing sleep, plus cognitive impairment or orthostatic intolerance.
takeaways: there is no blood test that confirms me/cfs
post-exertional malaise is a required feature
symptoms must substantially reduce activity for over 6 months
diagnosis is a doctor's call after other causes are checked
title: ME/CFS: a clinical diagnosis built on core symptoms
